Subject: Planning migration of internal namespace to Redwood Private — questions on DNS & trust

Hi Michael,

We're planning to migrate a set of internal services (currently under ai-internal.acme.local and svc.internal.acme) to Redwood Private hostnames reachable from our VPCs. Before we book a migration window I wanted to check a few design questions so we can prep our infra: 

- DNS: does Redwood prefer a delegated private zone (NS delegation into your private resolvers) or that we set up conditional forwarding to a Redwood resolver IP? Pros/cons from your side?
- TLS / trust: we run an internal CA (AcmeCorpRoot) for internal certs. Can Redwood accept a customer-provided root/trust bundle, or do you require us to issue leaf certs to you? What's your recommended rotation strategy so we don't cause mass trust failures?
- OCSP / CRL: we worry about OCSP availability from private endpoints. What's Redwood's stance on OCSP stapling for private certs?
- Cutover rollback: if we flip DNS and need to revert quickly, what do you recommend for TTLs or fallback?

We can provide network diagrams and the zone map if helpful. Looking for a short recommendation and suggested cutover checklist — pilot target week of Sep 24 if feasible.

Thanks,
Priyanka Shah

Subject: Re: Planning migration of internal namespace to Redwood Private — questions on DNS & trust

Hi Priyanka — thanks for the context. High-level answers below and we'll follow up with a detailed proposal & checklist.

1) DNS options (quick):
  - NS delegation (hidden/partial delegation into a Redwood-managed private zone): cleanest from a name ownership POV; you delegate an FQDN (or subdomain) to our resolver IPs. Pros: Redwood can manage TTLs, pre-warm caches, and run validation hooks. Cons: needs coordination on zone records and occasional ownership handoffs.
  - Conditional forwarding / VPC resolver endpoints: less record-handoff; your resolver forwards queries for ai-internal.* to Redwood. Pros: easy rollback (stop forwarding); cons: slightly more complexity for split-horizon and multi-region routing.

2) Trust model (quick):
  - We support customer-supplied root bundles (you upload a PEM bundle to your Private config). Redwood can either consume that as a trust anchor and issue intermediate certs, or accept leaf cert uploads.
  - For rotation I recommend short-lived leaf certs (30–90 days) issued by an intermediate that Redwood can rotate independently. Cross-sign overlap strategy is safest for cutovers.

3) OCSP / CRL: stapling in private nets is fragile if clients can't reach OCSP responders. For private environments we recommend either short-lived leaf certs (so revocation is rare) or an internal CRL distribution point reachable by clients. Redwood can enable OCSP stapling if you can expose an OCSP responder in a way reachable by our runtime.

4) Rollback: use low TTLs (30–300s) for A/AAAA/CNAMEs during cutover and prefer conditional-forwarding if you want fast rollback. If you must delegate NS records, plan a pre-cutover TTL reduction for parent zone and keep a pre-cutover resolver in place for 24–48h.

I'll loop Laura to provide a concrete step-by-step and attach a zone-mapping diagram + checklist.

—Michael

Subject: Proposal: zone migration approach & rotation play for ai-internal domains (detailed)

Hi Priyanka + team,

Thanks for the note — attached is a short proposal and a diagram that shows both options. TL;DR recommendation: start with conditional forwarding pilot, then migrate to a delegated private zone once we've validated behavior and telemetry. Rationale: fast rollback for pilot, then better operational ownership for long-term.

Key details (please read):

Option A — Conditional forwarding (pilot):
- Configure your VPC resolvers (or on-prem resolvers) to forward queries for ai-internal.acme.local and svc.internal.acme to Redwood VPC resolver endpoints (we'll provide a per-region IP set).
- Redwood publishes a private-resolver IP set and authoritative answers for those names.
- Pilot benefits: immediate rollback by removing forward; no NS changes in the parent zone; lower blast radius.
- Pilot caveat: split-horizon clients with multiple resolvers need consistent forwarders; we recommend testing from all client subnets.

Option B — Hidden NS delegation (long-term):
- You add NS records in the parent zone delegating the subdomain to the Redwood private name servers (we provide glue in the private resolver).
- Redwood assumes management of leaf records (we can accept record provisioning via API or zone file import).
- Benefits: single source-of-truth, Redwood can tune TTLs and pre-warm caches, easier cross-region failover.

Trust & certificate lifecycle (recommended):
- Customer-supplied trust anchor: you upload AcmeCorpRoot.pem to the Private deployment config. Redwood will validate chain on leaf certs and will generate per-service intermediates signed by a Redwood-managed intermediate that is cross-signed by AcmeCorpRoot for a smooth rotation.
- We propose the following rotation model: 
  1) Create a Redwood-managed intermediate signed by AcmeCorpRoot (one-time).
  2) Issue short-lived (45-day) leaf certs from the intermediate (automated via ACME sidecar or Redwood API).
  3) When rotating root or intermediate, overlap old and new intermediates for 7–14 days to avoid validation failures.
- If you prefer to retain full CA control, you can push leaf certs into Redwood via our API and we will keep them in your customer-managed KMS (we do not export private keys).

OCSP / revocation guidance:
- For private-only workloads, we recommend short-lived leaf certs + renewal automation over OCSP. If you require revocation semantics, host an internal OCSP responder reachable from Redwood runtime over private peering and we will enable stapling. Must-Staple is discouraged for private deployments unless the OCSP path is fully reachable.

Cutover checklist (high level):
1) Pilot (conditional-forwarding) — 72h: low TTLs on parent zone, configure forwarders from test VPCs, validate from clients, run smoke & perf tests.
2) Validate cert issuance: exchange test leaf cert, run TLS handshake tests including stapling.
3) Promote to production: if successful, schedule hidden NS delegation change with pre-reduced TTLs and monitor for 48–72h.
4) Rollback: remove conditional-forwarding or restore parent TTLs & resolvers as needed.

Attachments: redwood-private-dns-proposal.pdf (detailed diagram + phased plan), acme-zone-map.vsdx (your zone map labeled for planning). I've uploaded a checklist doc to the shared Drive: https://drive.google.com/file/d/1ExampleRedwoodProposal

We'll plan a dry-run with your SREs on Sep 24 weekend if that still works. Please confirm which option you want to pilot.

Thanks,

Quick TLS ops notes from the Infra-SRE perspective: 

- Client auth / mTLS: if you plan to use mTLS for service-to-service auth, you need a distribution path for client certs. For private deployments we usually recommend issuing short-lived client certs via an internal provisioning service (e.g., Vault PKI) and using SDS (Secret Discovery Service) to push certs into clients. Redwood supports mTLS if you provide client CA bundles and we can validate presented certs during handshake.
- OCSP stapling: as Laura mentioned, stapling is optional. Don't enable Must-Staple for private leaf certs. If you insist on revocation checks, an internal CRL + frequent updates is more predictable in an air-gapped/private environment.
- DNS TTL strategy: set parent zone TTLs to 300s for the week of cutover; reduce to 60s in the immediate pre-cutover window. After everything is stable, relax to 3600s.

I've drafted a short rotation-checklist that covers cert overlap windows, OCSP test steps, and SDS push verification. Attaching rotation-checklist.md.

—Kimberly Park
Security & Reliability Engineer, Redwood Inference

Priyanka — next steps and answers inline: 

- Forwarder failure/fallback: in the conditional-forwarding pilot, queries will failover based on your resolver behaviour. If your resolvers have multiple forwarders configured, clients will try the next one. We recommend configuring two forwarder endpoints (primary + warm standby) and enabling EDNS path MTU checks. For hidden NS delegation (long-term) Redwood offers cross-region authoritative endpoints so individual region loss doesn't drop resolution — that model has stronger HA characteristics.
- Coexistence with your internal CA: yes — Redwood will only trust the uploaded AcmeCorpRoot for the delegated subdomain. Non-Redwood services that use the same CA remain unaffected. We will not modify your parent zone records without explicit change requests.
- Pilot runbook: we'll produce a runbook that lists the exact API calls and pre-signed certs we'll upload, plus a timeline for TTL changes and smoke tests. I'll share the runbook and pre-requisite checks by EOD Sep 22.

Confirmed: we will do a conditional-forwarding pilot on Sep 24 (window 02:00–06:00 UTC). Owners: Acme SRE (Priyanka) for enabling forwarders + rollback; Redwood (Laura + Michael) for provisioning resolver endpoints, issuing test leafs, and running smoke tests.

I'll attach the runbook link once it's uploaded to the shared Drive. Thanks — we'll coordinate a 30-min pre-run call on Thu Sep 23 to walk through the steps.
